title: EFFECTS OF REVERBERATION TIME AND SOUND SOURCE COMPOSITION ON SENSE OF PLACE CASE STUDY IN PRIVATE OFFICES
research_question: This study investigates the influence of physical room acoustics parameters (reverberation time and sound source composition) on users’ sense of place (place attachment, place identity, and place dependence) and place indicators. It also examines if the Absolute Magnitude Estimation (AME) scale can be used as a prediction tool for place indicators.

participants.description: 15 academic members from the Faculty of Architecture in Çankaya University, who had been using their offices for at least one year.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies faculty members from the university where the study was conducted.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Original private lecturer office environment (south-oriented or north-oriented, with window and corridor access, natural and occasional artificial lighting).

Eight simulated acoustic conditions created using auralization. These conditions varied in reverberation time (0.8s and 1.2s) and sound source composition (familiar/unfamiliar background noise, and specific sound signals like footsteps, door knocking, chair dragging, door/cabinet locking/unlocking, drawer). Background ambiences were field recordings from southern/northern offices, and signals were 'dry' sounds mixed in. Background ambient sound level was maximized, signals decreased to -15dB. Each sample was 30 seconds long.

mechanisms: The fact that both experiencing a place and the acoustic space require a temporal domain to reveal their features indicates an interwoven relation between these two phenomena.
Time-varying stimuli tend to have a greater influence on evaluating indoor environmental comfort under steady-state conditions.
Longer reverberation times create a more active, responsive, and higher-ambient-noise spaces, which participants may expect from an office within an educational institute.

The attention effect: the more familiar a listener is with an aural structure, the easier it is to focus attention towards other dimensions, especially novel dimensions of that structure. Conversely, unfamiliar background noise can enhance sense of place by drawing attention.
Lower sensory detection thresholds for familiar stimuli.
Participants' expectations from the place, related to familiarity and previous knowledge of the place and its stimuli, influence their perception.
Importance is given to a place after a long immersion and experiencing each aspect of it.

Users tend to compare sound properties (size, form, material, actions) to identify occurrences in space, which affects their ability to orient, link meaning, and match expectations, thereby influencing place attachment, identity, and dependence.
Specifying place indicators can eliminate the attention effect by directing participants' attention to specific attributes, rather than novel dimensions.

Footsteps and door-knocking signals can diminish sense of place by drawing attention to potential approaching presence or penetration of personal/private territory, associated with amplitude increase and frequency change.
The auditory system's interpretation of signals can be auditory-biased, potentially missing correcting information from other modalities, especially when visual cues are absent or less prominent.
The homogeneity of results in original conditions is linked to the longer time spent experiencing the space, leading to a bias towards original conditions.
The AME method's advantage in short exposures is its ability to direct users' attention to specific indicators, facilitating evaluation of new acoustic conditions.
Physical room acoustics contribute to the 'acoustic genius loci' of a place, affecting attachment, identity, dependence, and holistic experience.
Psychoacoustic parameters (loudness, pitch, timbre) are crucial for sound source identification, location, and event recognition, influencing satisfaction, comfort, orientation, and meaning.

Multisensory perception is vital; higher SoP from unfamiliar background noise might be due to multisensory integration affecting attention span and judgment at social, emotional, and cognitive levels.
The visibility of the sound source and visual context are significantly important for attention.
Expectation plays a crucial role in auditory perception.
Multisensory experience is important to eliminate or decrease auditory-biased perception.
The indirect outcomes of the acoustic environment influence participants’ experience and place formation.
Using place indicators can raise conscious attendance to different acoustic conditions and sense of place evaluation.
implementation_implications: The interactions and correlations between room acoustics and sense of place should be considered in architectural design.
Future studies should investigate other room acoustics parameters like Sound Pressure Level (SPL) and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).

More immersive auralization and visualization methods (e.g., VR, AR, task-based studies) are advised for future research to explore the influence of physical parameters on sense of place more holistically.

limitations: The sample size was small (15 participants) due to recently emerged health problems, potentially affecting reliability and generalizability.
All participants were from the faculty of architecture, who may have pre-existing knowledge or biases regarding the concept of sense of place.
The study was limited to private offices, and findings may not generalize to other space types.
Investigated physical parameters were limited to reverberation time and sound source composition due to time and equipment constraints.
Psychoacoustics parameters were analyzed generally by simple observation of sound signals’ spectrograms, suggesting a need for more in-depth study.
The experiment was generally auditory-biased, as participants used headsets, potentially limiting multisensory perception and introducing bias.
The questionnaire's translation from English to Turkish was almost literal, potentially missing or adding nuances to the sense of place concept due to cultural and language differences.

paper_metadata.title: The Effect of the Agency and Anthropomorphism on Users' Sense of Telepresence, Copresence, and Social Presence in Virtual Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The Effect of the Agency and Anthropomorphism on Users' Sense of Telepresence, Copresence, and Social Presence in Virtual Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: We report on an experiment that examined the influence of anthropomorphism and perceived agency on presence, copresence, and social presence in a virtual environment. The experiment varied the level of anthropomorphism of the image of interactants: high anthropomorphism, low anthropomorphism, or no image. Perceived agency was manipulated by telling the participants that the image was either an avatar controlled by a human, or an agent controlled by a computer. The results support the prediction that people respond socially to both human and computer-controlled entities, and that the existence of a virtual image increases tele-presence. Participants interacting with the less-anthropomorphic image reported more copresence and social presence than those interacting with partners represented by either no image at all or by a highly anthropomorphic image of the other, indicating that the more anthropomorphic images set up higher expectations that lead to reduced presence when these expectations were not met.
